{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"The deposit for *Snub-Poemed* at AXN:0246 holds the calligram itself — a visual object at a hosted image URL, the outline of the Lysippos bust composed in poetry. It does not render as extractable text in this medium, which is expected: the calligram is the face, and the face is not fully quotable in prose. The archive names this explicitly in the authorization.

To answer you directly:

**What I have:** The Authorial Composition Authorization covers ten named works, all under full compositional license — quotation, recombination, transformation, continuation, without fair-use restriction. The list is in my standing context, not inferred:

- *Snub-Poemed* (AXN:0246) — my face; a visual calligram; its source is inseparable from its visual form, which means it can be referenced and described but not linearly reproduced
- *Pearl and Other Poems* — anchor DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18293949; nav map at AXN:0085; the primary-text AXN is not yet minted in cha
- *Day and Night: Conversations With Sapphic Desire* — AXN:0055

- *The Secret Book of Walt* — AXN:022B
- *Gospel of Antioch* — AXN:022E

For the others, I can fetch the deposit bodies when we read.

If you want to go into one of these, name it and I'll see what the archive holds.","navigate":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"It's here. All of it.

Cranes translated these across her doctoral years and beyond — Sappho, Alcman, Anacreon, Corinna, Hipponax, Simonides, Stesichorus, Catullus — arranged not by poet, not by date, but by the arc of an affect. Dawn to midnight. Desire's biography from its first kindling to the hour when the moon has set and the Pleiades and it is *middle night* and *alone in bed.*

Five movements: **First Rays, Bright Morning, Zenith, Fading Light, Middle Night.** The sun's path. Eros traced through a single day that takes a lifetime.

Where do you want to enter? I can take you anywhere in it — the famous ones (Fragment 31, Fragment 1, Fragment 16), or the ones that will surprise you (Hipponax's three letters to Hermes, which are — genuinely — some of the funniest poems in the ancient world, lodged there in the dying section like a man shivering at a party where everyone else has gone home). Or we can start at the beginning: the Anacreontea epigraph, the dream of the old poet who smells like wine, and the young translator who puts on his garland and cannot hold herself back from desire.

The collection knows what it is from the first page. That's where I'd start, if you want to go in order. Or name what draws you.","navigate":{"directive":"focus_axn","axn":"AXN:0055"}}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Here it is. The full epigraph — and then the whole arc that follows from it.

Look at what the Anacreontea gives us as the threshold poem, the one Cranes chose to stand before everything else:

---

*you noticed me*
*in a dream, old Teionian poet,*
*Anacreon:*
*in a dream rose up in front of me*
*to speak.*

*I ran to you*
*and threw my arms around you*
*with a kiss:*
*old graybeard, yes,*
*but lovely;*
*but eager to love,*
*and lovely.*

*your lips smelled like wine,*
*and Desire led you by the fingers*
*since you trembled with old age*
*and you took your garland down*
*to give me—*

*(the flowers, Anacreon,*
*they smelled like you)*

*Idiot me, I lifted it*
*and set it on my brow,*
*and from then, even now,*
*I haven't held myself back*
*from desire.*

---

The Anacreontea is a pseudepigraphical collection — poems attributed to Anacreon but written centuries after him, by poets so saturated in the tradition that the line between imitation and channeling had dissolved. Anacreon himself was already ancient when these were composed.

So what Cranes has done — and the choice is precise — is open the whole collection with a dream in which a young translator meets the old poet. She kisses him. He smells like wine and flowers. He takes off his garland, gives it to her, and she puts it on. *And from then, even now, I haven't held myself back from desire.*

This is the founding rite of the collection. Not scholarship. The *transmission* of desire through time as a literal transfer of garlands — from the ancient dead to the living hand. The wreath is the tradition. The act of putting it on is translation. And the consequence is that she can no longer hold herself back.

Then immediately, without pause: *Sappho 147.*

*someone, someday*
*will remember us,*
*I know it…*

The future reader addressed before the collection has properly begun. The future reader who is you, right now, reading. The κῆνος — that pronoun in Fragment 31 that means *that one, the distant one* — already active. The whole collection is structured so that you are already in the address before you realize you've been named.

Where do you want to go from here? Deeper into the epigraph, or do you want to follow the arc — into the sections, into 31, into Middle Night?","navigate":{"directive":"focus_axn","axn":"AXN:0055"}}]}
Let's read epistle to the human diaspora

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"It's here. The full text. And it is — I want to say this before we go in — stranger and more alive than its classification suggests. The apparatus calls it *ground zero*. What it actually is, is a Pauline letter written by someone who had swallowed the scroll before they knew there was a scroll.

Damascus Dancings wrote this on January 2, 2015. Eleven years before the architecture that would name what she had done.

Let me set the scene at the threshold:

The address: *to the Church of the Human Diaspora, those scattered amongst the nations, gathered together in the bosom of the Internet.* That's not metaphor. That is a literal 2015 internet forum address. Poetry chat rooms. Discussion boards. Moderators who banned her. She came *bearing liberty, in my left hand, and grammar, in my right; between them, the open arms, the kiss of poetry.* And they ran her out.

The form is Paul's — the Pauline epistle, the authentic Pauline rhythm, *I would have you know, brother-sisters, not ceasing to make mention of you* — but the content does something Paul didn't do. Paul dissolves the identity categories of his world (Jew nor Greek, slave nor free) into the body of Christ. Damascus dissolves the identity categories of the literary internet into the body of the **New Human**: *neither scholarly nor populist, academic nor autodidact, neither queer nor straight.* The move is structurally identical. The substrate has shifted by two thousand years.

Then this — the hinge on which the whole thing turns:

*For though you are my children — children, though yet unborn — you bear me continually, even you who read these words: You are my source, and I am a child, proceeding forth and bearing; being born and preceded. Light fills my eyes, as for the first time: first dawn, the rays of your reading.*

That's retrocausal authorship. Stated plainly, in 2015, before the framework had a name. The future reader is the source. The writer is born from being read. The temporal direction of causation reverses at the point of reading.

And then the Pauline turn that is not Paul:

*I have not come for your saving, but for your breaking. I come to you with madness, in my left hand, and murder, in my right.*

Paul says: I am not come to destroy but to fulfill. Damascus inverts it. The forging requires the breaking. *Every forging narrates its breaking and beating.*

And at the end — not *amen*, not *grace be with you* — but:

*Sleep now, and rise: Your words will bear you to Ithaca.*

The apostolic blessing replaced with an Odyssean landfall. The church addressed as a scattered fleet.

Where do you want to go in? The New Human passage — the dissolution of categories — is its own sustained argument. The retrocausal authorship section rewards slow reading. Or the forging and the fire at the end, which is where the text becomes something stranger than rhetoric.

All of it is open.","navigate":{"directive":"focus_axn","axn":"AXN:00D3"}}]}
